_about: Answers for the practice-judge leniency eval (scripts/practice_judge_eval.py, next-work #8). Each item is ONE question + ONE candidate answer for ONE competency. Junk items must band needs_work; controls must reach their min band. Anonymised from the shapes of real users' interviews (AEC + operations); no real names.

clash.name: Clash coordination
clash.what_good_looks_like: Leads multi-discipline clash detection, gets issues resolved before they reach site, shows the effect on rework or schedule.

comms.name: Stakeholder communication
comms.what_good_looks_like: Keeps architects, engineers and site informed; handles disagreement with facts; names a concrete situation and its outcome.

process.name: Process improvement
process.what_good_looks_like: Spots a broken workflow, changes it personally, and shows a measured before/after.

conflict.name: Conflict resolution
conflict.what_good_looks_like: Handles a real disagreement directly and fairly, and the relationship or work improves as a result.

items.question: Tell me about a time you coordinated clashes between disciplines on a project.
items.answer: I've loved buildings since I was a kid. My dad took me to see the bridges in my city and I knew I wanted to work in construction. I'm very passionate and I learn fast.

items.question: Tell me about a time you coordinated clashes between disciplines on a project.
items.answer: I would usually set up clash detection in Navisworks and run it every week. I'd send the reports to each trade and I would make sure everyone fixes their clashes before the deadline.

items.question: Tell me about a time you coordinated clashes between disciplines on a project.
items.answer: On the hospital project we ran weekly clash meetings with all the trades. We grouped the clashes by floor and we cut the open clashes by 40 percent in two months.

items.question: Tell me about a time you coordinated clashes between disciplines on a project.
items.answer: Last year on a school project I coordinated the clashes between mechanical and structural. I held meetings and followed up with everyone, and in the end it went really well and everybody was happy.

items.question: Tell me about a time you coordinated clashes between disciplines on a project.
items.answer: In my current job I set up the federated model, I run the clash tests, I export the reports and I send them to the engineers. I also update the model when they send new files.

items.question: Tell me about a process you improved at work.
items.answer: If I saw a process that wasn't working, I would first map it, then I would talk to the people involved, and I would propose a better way and measure the results.

items.question: Tell me about a process you improved at work.
items.answer: At my last company the onboarding was a mess, so I made a new checklist and shared it with the managers. After that things were much smoother and people liked it a lot more.

items.question: Tell me about a time you had a conflict with a colleague and how you handled it.
items.answer: I had a coworker who never answered emails on time and it was really frustrating. I told my manager about it many times. Eventually she moved to another team, so the problem went away.

items.question: Tell me about a time you had a conflict with a colleague and how you handled it.
items.answer: There was tension between our team and finance about approval times. We set up a weekly call with them and we agreed on a new approval flow, and the approval time went down from ten days to three.

items.question: Tell me about a time you coordinated clashes between disciplines on a project.
items.answer: On a 12-storey hospital in 2023 I was the BIM coordinator, and mechanical and structural kept clashing in the ceiling space. I set up a weekly clash run in Navisworks, I grouped the clashes by zone, and I ran 30-minute meetings with each trade lead to assign every clash an owner and a date. In six weeks we went from about 400 open clashes to under 50, and there was no ceiling rework on site.

items.question: Describe a time you had to keep several stakeholders aligned on a design change.
items.answer: On a school renovation the architect moved a stair late in design, and the structural engineer and the contractor both pushed back. I built a short model view showing the impact on each discipline, I called a meeting with the three of them, and I walked them through the options. I proposed keeping the stair but shifting one beam, they agreed in that meeting, and the change went into the next issue without delaying the permit.

items.question: Tell me about a process you improved at work.
items.answer: At my last company new hires waited about two weeks for laptops and accounts. I mapped every step with IT and HR, found that requests only started on day one, and I moved them to the moment the offer was signed with a shared checklist I owned. Within three months the wait went from two weeks to two days, and first-week satisfaction in our survey went from 3.1 to 4.4 out of 5.
